items.readable_text:
Content:
An inequality is a mathematical statement that represents a set of numbers on the number line. For example, the set of numbers that are greater than or equal to [MATH: 0] can also be represented by the inequality

Content:
[MATH: x \; {\color{red}\geq} \; 0]

Content:
Here, the sign [MATH: {\color{red}\geq}] means "greater than or equal to." So the above statement in words is "[MATH: x] is greater than or equal to zero." For example,

Content:
- the numbers [MATH: 0,] [MATH: 1,] and [MATH: 7.321] all satisfy the inequality, while
- the numbers [MATH: -0.01,] [MATH: -8,] and [MATH: -123] do not.

Content:
We can represent this inequality visually using a number line. To do so, we first plot the number zero as a red dot on the number line. The rest of the numbers that are greater than or equal to [MATH: 0] lie to the right of [MATH: 0,] so we represent them using a red line that extends to the right of [MATH: 0\mathbin{:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3346340489c98cb0a3ab0c8daeb16021]

Content:
In general, there are four types of inequalities:

Content:
> [MATH: \ge\quad] greater than or equal - this is represented by a filled circle [MATH: \Large\color{red}\bullet] and an arrow that goes to the right [MATH: \Large\color{red}\boldsymbol{\rightarrow}]
>
> [MATH: >\quad] greater than - this is represented by an empty circle [MATH: \Large\color{red}\circ] and an arrow that goes to the right [MATH: \Large\color{red}\boldsymbol{\rightarrow}]
>
> [MATH: \le\quad] less than or equal - this is represented by a filled circle [MATH: \Large\color{red}\bullet] and an arrow that goes to the left [MATH: \Large\color{red}\boldsymbol{\leftarrow}]
>
> [MATH: <\quad] less than - this is represented by an empty circle [MATH: \Large\color{red}\circ] and an arrow that goes to the left [MATH: \Large\color{red}\boldsymbol{\leftarrow}]

items.title: Constructing the Number Line for a Given Inequality

sections.normalized_html: Represent [MATH: x < -1] on a number line.
sections.readable_text: Represent [MATH: x < -1] on a number line.

sections.normalized_html:
The symbol "[MATH: <]" means "less than." So, the inequality [MATH: x < -1] represents the numbers that are less than [MATH: -1.]

On a number line, the numbers less than [MATH: -1] are the numbers that are left of [MATH: -1.] So, we should draw an arrow going to the left of [MATH: -1.]

However, the number [MATH: -1] itself is not less than [MATH: -1,] so we should not include it in our representation. To exclude [MATH: -1,] we draw an empty circle around [MATH: -1.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
An inequality is a mathematical statement that represents a set of numbers on the number line. For example, the set of numbers that are greater than or equal to [MATH: 0] can also be represented by the inequality

Content:
[MATH: x \; {\color{red}\geq} \; 0]

Content:
Here, the sign [MATH: {\color{red}\geq}] means "greater than or equal to." So the above statement in words is "[MATH: x] is greater than or equal to zero." For example,

Content:
- the numbers [MATH: 0,] [MATH: 1,] and [MATH: 7.321] all satisfy the inequality, while
- the numbers [MATH: -0.01,] [MATH: -8,] and [MATH: -123] do not.

Content:
We can represent this inequality visually using a number line. To do so, we first plot the number zero as a red dot on the number line. The rest of the numbers that are greater than or equal to [MATH: 0] lie to the right of [MATH: 0,] so we represent them using a red line that extends to the right of [MATH: 0\mathbin{:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3346340489c98cb0a3ab0c8daeb16021]

Content:
In general, there are four types of inequalities:

Content:
> [MATH: \ge\quad] greater than or equal - this is represented by a filled circle [MATH: \Large\color{red}\bullet] and an arrow that goes to the right [MATH: \Large\color{red}\boldsymbol{\rightarrow}]
>
> [MATH: >\quad] greater than - this is represented by an empty circle [MATH: \Large\color{red}\circ] and an arrow that goes to the right [MATH: \Large\color{red}\boldsymbol{\rightarrow}]
>
> [MATH: \le\quad] less than or equal - this is represented by a filled circle [MATH: \Large\color{red}\bullet] and an arrow that goes to the left [MATH: \Large\color{red}\boldsymbol{\leftarrow}]
>
> [MATH: <\quad] less than - this is represented by an empty circle [MATH: \Large\color{red}\circ] and an arrow that goes to the left [MATH: \Large\color{red}\boldsymbol{\leftarrow}]

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Inequality Represented by a Number Line

Example Prompt:
What inequality corresponds to the red colored graph shown in the number line below?

[IMG: /graphics/4ffe900b101eca2cd9d1be2a92f5072a]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The red arrow indicates that [MATH: x] should consist of all the values greater than [MATH: 2.] In addition, the filled red circle at [MATH: 2] implies that [MATH: x] can be equal to [MATH: 2.]

Therefore, the highlighted region represents the numbers that are greater than or equal to [MATH: 2.] This corresponds the inequality [MATH: x \geq 2.]

Item 5 — Example: Constructing the Number Line for a Given Inequality

Example Prompt:
Represent [MATH: x < -1] on a number line.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The symbol "[MATH: <]" means "less than." So, the inequality [MATH: x < -1] represents the numbers that are less than [MATH: -1.]

On a number line, the numbers less than [MATH: -1] are the numbers that are left of [MATH: -1.] So, we should draw an arrow going to the left of [MATH: -1.]

However, the number [MATH: -1] itself is not less than [MATH: -1,] so we should not include it in our representation. To exclude [MATH: -1,] we draw an empty circle around [MATH: -1.]
